lesson.text: You cannot secure what you do not see.

Attack surface defined: every point where an attacker can interact with a system. Village framing — gates, walls, sewer grates, fords — and their digital equivalents: endpoints, APIs, login forms, forgotten admin panels.
Defense-in-Depth — layered PREVENTATIVE (stop), DETERRENT (discourage), and DETECTIVE (observe & alert) controls. A system relying on prevention alone fails silently.
Some controls blur — a barking dog both deters AND alerts. Classify by the control's PRIMARY purpose, and when in doubt ask: does it STOP the act, or RECORD it?

Capability mapping: real threat modeling defends against the SPECIFIC actors capable of exploiting SPECIFIC gaps, not "everyone." Reference the Saboteur: high dexterity and stealth versus an unwatched lock on a cliff path.
In the field you'll find this as the West Gate. In an audit you'll find it as an unlogged service endpoint behind a default password.

quiz.q: A castle has a moat, a heavy iron gate, and a logbook recording everyone who enters. Which is the DETECTIVE control?
explain: Preventative — a physical barrier that stops the approach before it starts.
Preventative — an access barrier that stops entry before it starts.
Detective — the logbook records and reveals who came, enabling audit after the fact.
quiz.hint: Ignore what each control looks like doing — ask only which one leaves a record you'd check AFTER the fact, not before.

variant.q: A vault has a reinforced steel door, a silent alarm wired to motion sensors, and a bribed guard who waves people through. Which is the DETECTIVE control?
explain: Preventative — a physical barrier that stops entry before it starts.
Detective — the alarm doesn't stop anyone; it alerts you that someone got past the door.
This one's compromised, not a control at all — a bribed guard enforces nothing.

quiz.q: Your web app has a login page, a public API, and an old admin panel nobody remembers. Which is part of the attack surface?
explain: The attack surface isn't just the obvious front door.
The API matters, but it isn't the whole picture.
Attack surface = every interaction point, ESPECIALLY the forgotten ones — that is your West Gate.

quiz.q: The West Gate's lock sits on an unwatched cliff path with no lookout. Why is the Saboteur — high dexterity, high stealth — the real threat here, rather than whichever attacker happens to be strongest?
explain: Raw strength isn't what mattered here — the gap is a delicate lock, not a barred door.
Threat modeling maps actor capability to system gap; strength without fit is noise.
True, but that's a property of the location, not the threat actor — it's the fit between the two that matters.
